prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

Figure 4.3-4 Example of Walkway Lights 4.3.3 Pavement Surfacing 1. Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. On roads with overhead lines, medium-sized tree species that tolerate pruning should be selected. b. On life-service roads with heavy pedestrian flow, tree species whose mature fruits may fall and injure people or damage vehicles should not be selected. c. On roads with underground space or utility tunnels, shallow-rooted tree species should be selected. F. Flexible layout for special road dimensions 67 a. Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.

Facility requirements: • Provide convenient and safe pedestrian crossings; for life-service roads of higher grade, encourage elevated pedestrian crossings, curb extensions, and other traffic-calming facilities, and speed limits. • Encourage the use of green forms such as lawns, sparse tree stands, rows of trees, shrubs, and planting of trees and other vegetation to create a people-oriented, green environment. • Consider larger-canopy trees; for tall planting, the root space should be relatively small to ensure pedestrian passage space. • Use non-open interfaces on both sides as the main form; road greenery may be used to create transparent, screened, separated, and other visual-control effects. 9 Landscape-recreation roads Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • Encourage the integration of urban landscape and recreational functions, balancing landscape and leisure activities with residents’ daily travel needs. • Increase the amount of green space along the line to avoid vegetation becoming an obstacle to activities. Spatial requirements: • Roads of this type should combine waterfront space and roadside green space, and use connected green spaces and widened building setbacks to create street-side open spaces. • In areas with abundant road space, pedestrian and bicycle lanes or dedicated motor-vehicle and non-motorized lanes may be set up, with public facilities arranged on one side. • Encourage the use of “sea-sponge city” technology, using side ditches, median strips, and roadside green belts, as well as smart rainwater-management facilities, to shape block-like or belt-like forms and to regulate and purify rainwater. Facility requirements: • Use vegetation to shape different forms, emphasizing seasonal changes, increasing landscape layering, and enhancing road recognizability. • Select ornamental trees, flowers, and other plants, and arrange them in combination to strengthen the road’s distinctive character. • Encourage the setting of slow-mobility facilities such

Sidewalk paving: It shall meet the requirements of stability, anti-slip performance, flatness, ecological environmental protection, and urban landscape. Its design shall be practical, economical, aesthetically pleasing, and durable, and shall be designed for permeability in accordance with sponge city requirements. Guidance and directional signs may be added to the paving; signs shall be appropriately scaled and clearly informative. 2. Tactile paving: The color of tactile paving should contrast with the color of adjacent sidewalk paving and be coordinated with the surrounding landscape. The surface of tactile paving profiles shall have anti-slip functionality. The width should be 0.3 m–0.6 m, and the tactile pattern shall protrude 4 mm above the road surface. Tactile paving shall be laid continuously and shall avoid obstacles such as trees (tree pits), utility poles, and guy wires. Figure 4.3-5 Example of tactile paving 3. Curb stones: These shall be designed in accordance with road class, construction scale, landscape environment, and usage requirements. Sidewalks must be provided with curb ramps at all intersections and at the entrances/exits of residential communities and institutions fronting the street. The height difference between the curb stone and the road surface shall not exceed 1 cm. At pedestrian crossings, the centerline of the curb-ramp opening should align with the centerline of the crosswalk. At road intersections, curb ramps are recommended to adopt a full-width, single-sided ramp descending to the bottom. 4. Tree pits / tree grates: Their dimensions shall be designed in coordination with the sidewalk paving, forming a certain proportional modular relationship. The paved surface of the tree pit / tree grate should be flush with the sidewalk paving. Tree grates should preferably use fiberglass grating, eco-friendly rubber, stone paving, and similar materials. In parks, squares, commercial pedestrian streets, and other leisure activity areas, tree pits should be designed in combination with seating, or as compact / multifunctional designs that provide seating functions. Figure 4.3-6 Example of tree pits / tree grates 5. Manhole covers: All types of manhole covers shall comply with the relevant standards in Manhole Covers (GB/T 23858-2009). The paved surface of the manhole cover shall be flush with the sidewalk paving surface, and the height difference shall not exceed 1 cm. Concealed manhole covers may be used; the decorative surface layer shall be unified with the road paving. Manhole covers with distinctive patterns may also be used. Landscape-recreation roads Definition: roads with prominent landscape features, along which parks, green spaces, and recreational facilities are distributed. Design focus: create road scenes with smooth slow-mobility circulation, beautiful scenery, openness and transparency, and convenient facilities. Historic-style streets and lanes Definition: streets and lanes that preserve abundant cultural relics, concentrate historic buildings, can more completely reflect the traditional spatial pattern, and have a certain scale. Design focus: prioritize slow mobility, continue the historic and cultural character, and enhance vitality and activity. Smart-city demonstration roads Definition: roads that, through data technologies such as autonomous driving and vehicle-road coordination, achieve deep interaction among people, vehicles, and road space, and serve as a showcase and promotion of Suzhou’s smart-city characteristics. Design focus: based on an integrated framework of the traffic-participant subsystem, roadside subsystem, and central subsystem. Emphasis is placed on “the road” and “the cloud,” providing intelligent services for “vehicles” and “people.” Comprehensive roads Definition: roads with a relatively high degree of mixing between road functions and interface types, and with characteristics of two or more road types. Design focus: carry out targeted road design according to the requirements of multiple road-type characteristics. 7 Road-type functional traffic corridors Recommendations for upgrading and improving interface types General requirements: • The design should respond to the needs of different traffic modes, including motor vehicles, non-motorized traffic, public transport, freight transport, and pedestrian traffic, with a coordinated allocation of space. • At intersections where signal lights are installed, allow motor vehicles to pass with longer distances and higher speeds as much as possible, reducing crossings by motor vehicles and pedestrians. Spatial requirements: • Intersections should be organized in a clear and orderly manner; curb extensions may be set up, pedestrian crossing distances shortened, and pedestrian visibility improved. • The roadside interface should mainly be non-open, and road greenery, screens, separation, and transparent visual-control effects may be used.
